Appendix F
Qualitative Codebook, Case Audit, and In-
tegration Record
The coding unit is one supplied researcher-recorded encounter. Codes can co-
occur. Observations and recorded remarks supply evidence; researcher reections
supply contextual interpretation only. The full machine-readable codebook, case
memos, source hashes, and joined audit are preserved in the thematic codebook,
the case-level coding record, the coding-provenance record, and the mixed-methods
verication record.
T1: Grounds for credibility
Include source use, correction, neutrality, explanation, viewpoint diversity,
peer review, or ratings as explicit judgment cues. Exclude generic praise and
unqualied technical clarity.
T2: Peer connection
Include natural student speech, familiarity, friendship, authenticity, or solidar-
ity. Exclude an interface preference without a peer connection.
T3: Situated listening value
Include calm, fatigue, quiet appreciation, limited time, concision, structure, or

immersion. A recorded duration alone is insucient.
T4: Participatory agency
Include voting, topic control, creator aspirations, co-creation, privacy condi-
tions, or contribution to platform improvement. Distinguish recorded actions
from future intentions.
T5: Student-lived relevance
Include explicit campus, work, study, career, local-mobility, or civic interests.
Do not infer preferences from faculty membership alone.
T6: Enabling delivery and interface
Include experienced continuity, audio clarity, latency, visual integration, con-
trols, or usability. Do not code such praise as independently measured accuracy
or engineering quality.

F.1
Audit and Interpretive Scope
The coding was performed by the researcher and reviewed during thesis revision.
No independent-coder statistics, member checking, or saturation assessment were
performed for these 60 rider records. A separate 193-segment FGD/self-report code-
book validation is reported in Section 6.12.15. The coding matrix, source excerpts,
and case memos preserve the basis for examining alternative readings. The record
does not establish that every recorded remark is a verbatim transcript. Interpretive
disagreement is distinct from an error in recounting code frequencies. A numeri-
cal recount can reproduce the coding matrix; it cannot independently validate the
interpretive choices.
